method: Every saved active mathematical environment is indexed by its exact body label/hash, direct historical paragraph links and explicit internal proof dependencies. First manuscript read credit comes from the actual recorded source ranges, not parsing or successful builds. Indirect auxiliary-result historical contexts still require semantic adjudication; the index alone does not close H01 or certify proofs or originality. Source statement and source proof checks are recorded separately in the source ledger and existing scoped reviews.

history_paragraphs.text: Distribution theory interprets differentiation by duality against smooth tests. The local finite-order bound, mollification, and positivity-to-measure argument in \cref{def:distribution,prop:distribution-smoothing,thm:positive-distribution-measure} can be compared with \cite[Section 1, Exercises 4--5; Section 2, Definition 1, Exercise 15 and Lemma 2]{Tao09Distributions}. That source places the test function first and uses a conjugate complex structure on distributions. Our pairing is $\langle T,\chi\rangle=\int u\chi\,\mathrm d x$, complex linear in both variables, as required for the later current conventions. The derivative sign is the same after this conversion. The proof of \cref{prop:distribution-smoothing} includes the passage of Riemann sums through a distribution, rather than assuming that interchange.

The measure selection and compactness statements in \cref{thm:local-measure-selection,thm:local-measure-compactness} distinguish the countable test-family argument from compactness of a product of scalar intervals. The latter uses the axiom of choice, through the ultrafilter proof in \cref{lem:compact-product}. \Cref{prop:compact-net-characterization} gives the subnet construction for the precise Willard convention used throughout this book.

The Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem in \cref{prop:arzela-ascoli} is proved by finite nets in the compact domain and in the bounded range of point values. Equicontinuity upgrades approximation on those nets to uniform approximation. Completeness and the nested finite-net argument then give compactness of the uniform closure.

history_paragraphs.text: For differentiation of integrals compare \cite[Section 2, Theorems 32 and 36, Exercise 38 and Lemma 39]{Tao10Differentiation}. \Cref{thm:lebesgue-differentiation} uses cubes instead of balls: the finite disjoint selection still covers the original cubes by their threefold enlargements, giving the constant $3^d$. The approximation argument and the localization from $L^1$ to $L^1_{\loc}$ are written out. \Cref{lem:weak-poincare-cube} follows by integrating the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus along successive coordinate segments.

For the Radon--Nikodym theorem compare \cite[Corollary 1, following Theorem 2]{Tao09RN}. \Cref{lem:dominated-measure-density} proves the bounded-domination case relative to any positive Radon measure by a dyadic $L^2$ identity on compactly contained cubes. The half-open partitions do not require null cube boundaries, and uniqueness glues the local densities. This gives the coefficient densities needed in \cref{lem:bounded-psh-current-chain-rule} without importing the general Lebesgue decomposition theorem.

history_paragraphs.text: The Perron replacement argument, resolutivity for continuous boundary data, and barriers are developed in \cite[Section 3.3, pp.~171--174, especially Theorem 3.3.3, Definition 3.3.4 and Theorem 3.3.5]{Hor07}. \Cref{thm:perron-harmonic,thm:perron-resolutivity} use continuous subsolutions and prove the required maximum and replacement properties before forming the envelopes. The equivalence between regularity and barriers can also be compared with \cite[Theorem 3.4.17, pp.~219--220]{Hor07}. Our \cref{prop:local-barrier} assumes a continuous extension positive on the nearby boundary except at the distinguished point; it makes no claim about the more general exceptional sets considered there. The Green construction in \cref{thm:dirichlet-green} has the boundedness and boundary regularity assumptions at its point of use and proves the exhaustion limit within that class.

For compactness and Hartogs' lemma compare \cite[Theorems 3.2.12--3.2.13, pp.~149--151]{Hor07}. \Cref{thm:subharmonic-compactness,thm:hartogs-subharmonic} state the distributional-to-$L^1$ implication and the upper bound with a common local upper bound, and prove the integral estimates and convolution limit they use. They do not assert the stronger Sobolev or measure-weighted convergence results of Theorem 3.2.13. The countable selection and regularization argument in \cref{lem:choquet-selection,thm:subharmonic-envelope} corresponds to \cite[Proposition 3.4.4, pp.~205--206]{Hor07}; completed Lebesgue measurability is sufficient for the unrestricted pointwise supremum. The local definition of polarity and the removal argument in \cref{def:polar-set,thm:polar-removable} can be compared with \cite[Definition 3.4.1 and Theorem 3.4.3, pp.~203--205]{Hor07}. The proof here uses local polar functions directly and supplies the connectedness conclusion through the maximum principle.

history_paragraphs.text: Strong subadditivity, outer regularity and capacitability are developed in \cite[Section 3.4, pp.~209--216, especially Theorems 3.4.9 and 3.4.12 and Proposition 3.4.13]{Hor07}. The continuous-potential testing argument in \cref{lem:continuous-potential-testing} is the measure-testing part of \cite[Theorem 3.2.13, pp.~150--151]{Hor07}; the polar discrepancy conclusion in \cref{thm:polar-limit-discrepancy} corresponds to \cite[Theorem 3.4.14, pp.~216--217]{Hor07}. This continuation strengthens the almost-everywhere envelope equality proved in \cref{thm:subharmonic-envelope}.

\Cref{thm:choquet-capacitability} writes out the compact approximation for analytic sets underlying the capacitability assertion in that section. The empty target is handled first, and all parameter spaces in its countable product are nonempty.

For the Dirichlet identity and quasi-continuity compare \cite[Propositions 3.4.19 and 3.4.21, pp.~221--223]{Hor07}. \Cref{prop:bounded-green-energy} proves the $L^2$ gradient limit by a Cauchy argument and uses the explicitly symmetric ball Green kernel. Newtonian positivity and conditional logarithmic positivity in \cref{prop:kernel-energy-positivity} are proved separately by Gaussian integrals; the zero-mass restriction explains why an unrestricted logarithmic Cauchy--Schwarz inequality is not used. The minimization argument and \cref{prop:equilibrium-frostman} give the equilibrium characterization within these precise kernel conventions.

The atom-free polar-Cantor measure used in \cite[Example~6.1.3, labelled \texttt{ex:BBJ}]{XiaSampleBook} is supplied explicitly by \cref{prop:diffuse-polar-cantor-measure}. The source cites Carleson's book, p.~31, for its Cantor-set input. Our rapidly decreasing binary construction makes the measure's own logarithmic potential equal to $-\infty$ on its entire support. \Cref{prop:projective-logarithmic-measure-potential,cor:zero-lelong-trivial-multiplier-ideal,ex:diffuse-polar-zero-nonpluripolar-mass} give the spherical potential, integrability and first-degree mass calculation underlying that example.

The compact reduction and sweeping statements in \cref{thm:compact-reduction,thm:compact-balayage,thm:finite-energy-balayage} use the symmetric Green kernel of a ball and the finite-energy identity proved in \cref{prop:finite-green-energy}. Orthogonality determines the swept measure and proves additivity; the manuscript does not use the unproved general axiomatic duality recalled by that source. The harmonic-measure formula in \cref{ex:balayage-harmonic-measure} retains the stated boundary regularity. The topological example in \cref{prop:classical-plurifine-distinction} distinguishes the real subharmonic generating class from the complex-line class directly, without transferring fine connectedness results to the latter.

For the dyadic decomposition compare \cite[Proposition 4.3 and proof, pp.~23--24]{Tao06Fourier3}; for the weak $(1,1)$ estimate and its interpolation and adjoint consequences compare \cite[Lemma 2.7, Corollaries 2.9--2.10 and proofs, pp.~7--9]{Tao06Fourier4}. \Cref{lem:hessian-multiplier-kernel} constructs only the Hessian multipliers needed here, from differentiated heat kernels. \Cref{lem:hessian-multiplier-weak-one,thm:hessian-multiplier-lp} give the complete cancellation and distribution-function argument, including the adjoint passage above $p=2$. \Cref{lem:gradient-lp-interpolation,lem:morrey-sobolev-representative} supply the interpolation and continuous-representative estimates used in the metric-Laplacian application.

The annular-star, complex-hyperplane projection and incidence arguments reconstruct \cite[Lemmas 1.3--1.5, pp.~2--4]{PSHD}. That manuscript has no printed author or publication information. \Cref{lem:positive-circle-selection} supplies an explicit Borel selector for the actual closed high-value circle sections: the submean inequality gives them positive arc length, so an arc-length median suffices. No general compact-section uniformization theorem is needed for this argument. The invariant measures are constructed from Gaussian matrices, and the projective ball estimate replaces an appeal to manifold volume charts. \Cref{cor:borel-line-subharmonic-bound} retains Borel measurability as a hypothesis; the subsequent complex-line characterization must supply it before applying that result.

history_paragraphs.text: The general linear mixed Hodge--Riemann theorem of Timorin is recorded in \cite[Proposition 2.1, p.~4]{DN2005mixedv2}. \Cref{lem:mixed-discriminant-signature} proves its real $(1,1)$ signature case by principal-minor induction and deformation to the identity matrices. Its pairing is the wedge intersection pairing, with its sign determined directly by the trace formula.

For local potentials compare \cite[Chapter III, Section 1.18 and (1.19), p.~135]{DemBook}. \Cref{thm:local-positive-current-potential} supplies a different proof through the scalar trace potential and a harmonic trace-free remainder; only the smooth local exactness of \cref{lem:smooth-dbar-poincare} is required. The pointwise composition assertion in \cref{prop:positive-hessian-holomorphic-composition} uses radial regularization of the canonical subharmonic representative.

The contour preparation proof in \cite[Chapter II, Section 2.A, pp.~79--80, Theorem (2.1)]{DemBook} is attributed there to Siegel; it gives \cref{thm:local-weierstrass-preparation}. The divisor identity is \cite[Chapter III, (2.15), pp.~143--144]{DemBook}: its $(\mathrm{i}/\pi)\partial\bar\partial\log|f|$ equals our $\ddc\log|f|^2$, while its subsequent $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}$ is twice ours. In \cref{thm:poincare-lelong}, coordinate slices and \cref{lem:divisor-exceptional-projections} give the singular divisor locus zero Hessian mass, identifying weighted regular-sheet integration with the logarithmic Hessian. The quotient example gives the meromorphic identity in $L^1_{\loc}$.

The distributional, envelope and compactness assertions in \cref{thm:psh-distribution-representative,thm:psh-upper-envelopes,thm:psh-compactness-hartogs} use the real subharmonic foundations of \cref{chap:p03,chap:p04}. The discrepancy conclusion at this stage is real polarity in charts. The extension criterion \cref{thm:psh-small-set-extension} proves both local boundedness and removal from a Hausdorff-null hypothesis; translating analytic codimension into that hypothesis requires the local dimension estimate for analytic sets.

history_paragraphs.text: For finite-$p$ integrability and convergence, compare \cite[Theorem 1.48, parts 1--2 and proof Steps 1--2, pp.~30--32]{GZ17}. \Cref{lem:negative-subharmonic-disc-lp,prop:negative-psh-polydisc-lp,thm:psh-local-lp-integrability} use the same one-variable-to-polydisc mechanism, with compactly supported Riesz decomposition in place of a boundary Poisson--Jensen formula. Our Riesz measure is $\Delta v$, so its logarithmic potential has coefficient $1/(2\pi)$. The norm bound \eqref{eq:negative-psh-lp-lone-bound} gives uniformity directly on smaller polydiscs. H\"older interpolation proves convergence; the equality with factor two in the printed truncation display on p.~32 is false, as also observed in the supplied unofficial reader errata.

The local exponential estimates in \cref{lem:negative-subharmonic-disc-exponential,prop:negative-psh-ball-exponential} follow from the same compact Riesz decomposition: Jensen's inequality controls an inverse-power kernel on the disc, and polar integration averages the complex-line estimates through one finite point. Their exponent depends only on a local $L^1$ bound. The global normalized version in \cref{cor:normalized-global-psh-exponential-bound} then uses compactness and a finite chart cover.

history_paragraphs.text: The partial Legendre transformation is due to Kiselman \cite{Kis78}. The invariant minimum principle and its regularization argument are developed in \cite[Chapter I, Section 7.B, Theorem (7.5) and its proof, p.~57]{DemBook}. \Cref{thm:kiselman-invariant-exhaustion} makes the invariant exhaustion an explicit hypothesis and proves the smooth case by a Schur complement. \Cref{cor:kiselman-product-tube} constructs such an exhaustion for every open convex product tube. The general pseudoconvex-tube statement additionally needs the plurisubharmonic boundary-distance criterion.

history_paragraphs.text: For increasing continuity, maximum locality and comparison compare \cite[Theorem 3.23, pp.~89--91, and Theorems 3.27 and 3.29, pp.~93--94]{GZ17}. Capacity, quasi-continuity and capacity convergence appear in \cite[Proposition 4.19, Theorem 4.20 and Lemma 4.21, pp.~110--112, and Theorem 4.26, pp.~114--115]{GZ17}. The capacity normalization uses competitors between zero and one. Both cited sources use $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}=(\mathrm{i}/\pi)\partial\bar\partial$, twice our operator, so their $n$-fold measure and capacity are $2^n$ times ours. The local domination proof in \cref{cor:bt-local-domination} reconstructs the supplied psh chapter's Proposition \texttt{dom\_prin\_loc} by strict quadratic perturbation and comparison on a relatively compact strict sublevel set.

The difference estimate is attributed to B\l{}ocki in \cite[Proposition 3.21, pp.~88--89]{GZ17}. Its printed oscillation power $M^{n+1}$ must be $M^n$: there are $n$ integration-by-parts substitutions, and the left side has degree $n$ in the test potential. \Cref{prop:blocki-difference-estimate} proves that power under an explicit common-collar hypothesis and passes to bounded potentials by polynomial-weight continuity. \Cref{cor:psh-envelope-zero-capacity} gives the capacity-zero discrepancy needed to identify exceptional envelopes with pluripolar sets.

The homogeneous Dirichlet construction goes back to \cite{BT76}. The exact-center automorphism averaging is developed for polydiscs in \cite[Section 2.3, Theorem 2.3.2 and Proposition 2.3.3, pp.~50--52]{Blo02Pluripotential}; \cref{lem:ball-centered-automorphisms} gives its ball version. Compare also \cite[Theorems 5.13--5.14, pp.~143--149]{GZ17}. \Cref{prop:bounded-hessian-taylor} proves the almost-everywhere Taylor expansion needed to identify the determinant, using differentiation of integrals and the cube Poincar\'e estimate. The canonical replacement in \cref{cor:homogeneous-psh-balayage} is the largest boundary-envelope solution for a locally bounded potential. \Cref{thm:bounded-psh-maximality} uses that replacement and bounded comparison; its local conclusion concerns locally bounded functions.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
The upper-test characterization and determinant linearization are proved in \cite[Proposition 1.5 and Lemma 1.7, pp.~5--7]{EGZ10ViscosityV1}, the exact first arXiv version of the later article by Eyssidieux--Guedj--Zeriahi. \Cref{lem:constant-elliptic-upper-tests} supplies the harmonic-comparison and distributional bridge quoted there from H\"ormander. The source's trace matrices have determinant $n^{-n}$; multiplying them by $n$ gives our determinant-one matrices. \Cref{prop:bounded-monge-ampere-linear-density} measures the density against $(\ddc|z|^2)^n$. The smooth mixed inequality and its bounded Lebesgue-density extension are stated in \cite[Theorems 1.1--1.2, pp.~1--2]{Din07MixedV1}; the latter is attributed there to Ko\l{}odziej and B\l{}ocki. \Cref{cor:bounded-mixed-continuous-density} proves the continuous-density case internally by linearization and decreasing convolution. Dinew's displayed smooth measure is $(4\pi)^n$ times ours at fixed potentials. \Cref{cor:bounded-common-measure-mixed} supplies the bounded common-measure case below.

\Cref{thm:continuous-density-ball-dirichlet} reconstructs the ball Dirichlet argument in \cite[Theorems 5.13--5.14 and Corollary 5.15, pp.~143--149]{GZ17}. Its exact-center automorphisms remove the preliminary Lipschitz comparison with translations. The pullback root is $(f^{1/n}\circ S)|\det_{\mathbb C}DS|^{2/n}$; the absolute value and the derivative are essential. The symmetric error is quadratic, and the half-sum is taken only once, correcting the printed formulas on pp.~145--146. The stability estimate \eqref{eq:ball-dirichlet-root-stability} retains the boundary-data error omitted on p.~149 and needs no monotone approximation of two different kinds of data. The density is relative to $\eta^n=(\ddc|z|^2)^n$; at fixed potentials the source operator gives $2^n$ times our measures.

\Cref{lem:local-comparison-capacity-sublevels,thm:bounded-density-ball-dirichlet} give the bounded-density continuation in \cite[Theorem 5.17 and Lemma 5.18, pp.~150--151]{GZ17}. The comparison estimate uses strict level sets and only requires compact containment of the shifted set. The approximating densities have an explicit common bound. Hartogs\textquoteright{} lemma is applied on compact subsets outside the quasi-continuity exception; the opposite difference is controlled by that common bound and $L^1$ convergence. This proves local capacity convergence without assuming interior continuity of the measurable-density solution. Root convolution also extends \eqref{eq:ball-dirichlet-root-stability} to this regime.

Cegrell's bounded zero-boundary class is recalled in \cite[Section 2, p.~3]{Din07MixedV1}. The moment condition used for canonical approximation is stated there in Theorem~2.2, pp.~4--5; its approximation and stability conclusions are quoted from other sources. \Cref{thm:bounded-subsolution-local-energy-moments} proves the moment condition for measures dominated by a bounded local subsolution, directly from our earlier B\l{}ocki estimate and layer integration. Its common collar is obtained on a smaller ball after truncating the zero-boundary test potential. The constants retain the measure mass and subsolution oscillation, and the estimate also holds in dimension one. \Cref{prop:canonical-grid-energy-control} combines the earlier local $L^p$ bound with half-open cube averages to preserve that criterion. Testing it on each zero-boundary solution gives uniform local energy moments, and the quadratic reference measure gives $L^1$ subsequential compactness. At fixed potentials Dinew's operator scales measures and local energy moments by $(4\pi)^n$; the measure-mass factor in \eqref{eq:local-energy-measure-moment} gives the same overall scaling.

The self-integral convergence is asserted in \cite[Theorem 2.2(3), p.~5]{Din07MixedV1}, where it is quoted from Cegrell. \Cref{thm:canonical-grid-self-integral-convergence} proves the compactly supported bounded-subsolution case for any volume $L^1$-convergent subsequence. In \cref{lem:bounded-psh-fixed-measure-continuity}, minimum-norm convex tail combinations and the capacity-zero envelope discrepancy give continuity against a fixed measure. The finite-center local $L^p$ estimate then controls cell averages. Hartogs' lemma bounds their positive error, while the uniform second moment controls the negative tails and turns convergence in measure into convergence of the energy integrals.

Capacity stability from the self-integral error is quoted in \cite[Theorem 2.3, p.~5]{Din07MixedV1}. \Cref{thm:canonical-grid-capacity-convergence} derives it here from the earlier strict sublevel comparison and second-moment tails. The comparison uses the zero boundary value of each approximant and the nonpositivity of the limit. \Cref{lem:zero-boundary-truncation-mass} obtains exact mass preservation by a compact-support current identity; it controls both the deep-set measure error and uniform absolute continuity with respect to capacity. The finite mass and total variation estimate for the limit's bounded truncations follow by bounded-product continuity and continuous approximation of Borel tests.

citations.locator: Definition 2.4 and the following paragraph, p.~5

history_paragraphs.text: The subsolution envelope is recalled in \cite[Definition 2.4 and the following paragraph, p.~5]{Din07MixedV1}. \Cref{thm:compact-bounded-subsolution-ball-dirichlet} proves the compact-support, zero-boundary case on a ball. A maximum with a quadratic potential supplies a bounded barrier. Capacity-controlled weights and fixed-measure energy continuity pass comparison to the canonical limit at null levels of both finite measures. A strict quadratic perturbation then bounds the limit and supplies its boundary trace; finite-mass comparison proves the envelope and uniqueness.

The mixed energy inequalities used in the approximation argument are recorded in \cite[Section 2, p.~4]{Din07MixedV1} and attributed there to Cegrell. The integration-by-parts and Cauchy--Schwarz mechanism can be compared directly with \cite[Lemma 5.4 and Theorem 5.5, pp.~168--170]{Ceg04}; the latter theorem keeps a fixed weight and has exponents $1/n$. \Cref{thm:bounded-mixed-local-energy} proves the $n+1$-energy bound needed here with an explicit, weaker constant. Quadratic boundary collars first permit full symmetry of the weighted integral; a finite multiplicity argument gives the constant-one bound in that class. A uniform maximum approximation and a strict sublevel comparison then control the energies for general bounded zero-boundary potentials. Both sides of the resulting inequality scale by the same $n$-th power under a positive rescaling of $\ddc$. \Cref{cor:mixed-products-energy-capacity-continuity} discards deep sets using this energy bound before applying bounded capacity continuity; no product of unbounded limit potentials is defined.

The bounded common-measure inequality is proved in \cite[Theorem 3.3, p.~9]{Din07MixedV1}. Its approximation proof, Proposition~3.1 and Lemma~3.2, pp.~7--9, relies on quoted local Dirichlet, energy and capacity-continuity results. \Cref{thm:bounded-multifactor-common-measure} extends the canonical-grid mechanism to $n$ independent potentials, with those inputs proved in the preceding sections. The reverse Cauchy inequality from \cref{lem:mixed-discriminant-signature} and a finite multiplicity argument prove \cref{lem:multifactor-mixed-discriminant}; pure density linearization then gives \cref{cor:bounded-multifactor-continuous-density}. Compactly supported pieces of all the pure measures first give zero-boundary solutions; finite-mass strict comparison identifies their decreasing limits. At a fixed compact piece, generalized H\"older's inequality on each cube gives the desired lower density, and energy-controlled mixed continuity passes it to the limit. A second limit exhausts the ball, and quadratic maximum collars localize arbitrary bounded potentials. The common Radon measure need not ignore pluripolar sets in this bounded case. The unbounded Cegrell-class extension in Theorem~3.4 is outside the scope of this local chapter.

The contact-set calculation in the supplied non-pluripolar chapter \cite[Lemma \texttt{DNTroof}, Step 1]{XiaSampleBook} invokes Stampacchia's zero-set locality, but also asserts a classical real Hessian from $W^{2,1}$ membership. Compare the complete argument in \cite[Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, pp.~4--8]{DNT2019v1}. That source defines $C^{1,\overline1}$ by a bounded metric Laplacian, rather than a bounded full real Hessian, and invokes elliptic $W^{2,p}$ regularity. \Cref{lem:weak-derivative-zero-set} proves weak locality directly by a smooth truncated chain rule; \cref{lem:bounded-laplacian-weak-hessian} obtains real $W^{2,2}$ derivatives for a bounded Euclidean Laplacian by a cutoff estimate and two integrations by parts. These supply \cref{prop:bounded-complex-hessian-contact,prop:bounded-complex-hessian-density} for regular potentials and weakly differentiable barriers. Their contact-restricted density needs no global determinant integrability for the barrier. The cited preprint uses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm i\partial\bar\partial$, which is $2\pi$ times our operator.

history_paragraphs.text: The positive-superlevel neighborhood base can be compared with \cite[Lemma 3.1, pp.~3--4]{EMW05Plurifine}, the retained arXiv version of the later article \cite{EMW06}. The submission and the date displayed by that PDF differ, as recorded in the bibliography. That source's local-connectivity theorem also uses finely subharmonic inputs; it is not used to prove the base or the quasi-Lindel\"of principle here. \Cref{thm:plurifine-quasi-lindelof} uses Choquet selection and the pluripolar discrepancy already proved. \Cref{thm:bt-plurifine-locality} derives local equality from bounded maximum locality, then removes only exceptions which bounded products do not charge. The common-pole and quasi-extremum assertions retain the pointwise domain on which subtraction is defined.

The bounded twist and local extension construction follow the method of Chen as presented in \cite[Theorems 9.1--9.3 and Lemma 9.4, pp.~46--48]{Blo14SCV}. \Cref{lem:extension-log-log-weight} uses the positive parameter $s=-\log(|\zeta|^2+\varepsilon^2)$ and differentiates $-\log(s+\log s)$ explicitly; the annulus agrees with the squared-radius cutoff. \Cref{thm:local-ot-extension} retains the singular pole, normal scaling and exhaustion limits. Its constant depends only on the normal radius, and iteration gives \cref{cor:ot-point-value-bound}.

Multiplier-ideal coherence and the Hilbert-space generation proof are presented in \cite[Proposition 5.7, pp.~36--37]{DemAnalyticOnline}; they give \cref{thm:multiplier-ideal-coherence}. Its weight $\mathrm e^{-2\varphi}$ becomes our $\mathrm e^{-\varphi}$ after doubling the potential. The strong Noetherian and Artin--Rees ingredients are \cite[Chapter II, (3.22), p.~90, and Chapter IX, (1.1)--(1.3), pp.~403--404]{DemBook}. \Cref{lem:strong-analytic-noetherian} supplies the finite-hypersurface direct-image matrix argument, and \cref{lem:bounded-hilbert-ideal-generation} makes uniform generation explicit by completeness of the Hilbert space.

Siu's analytic semicontinuity theorem originated in \cite{Siu74}. The multiplier-order proof used in \cref{thm:siu-lelong-level-sets} is Demailly's method; compare \cite[Corollary 14.3, p.~138]{DemAnalyticOnline} and \cite[Theorem 10.2 and Lemma 10.3, p.~42]{Bou23Notes}. The product and diagonal proofs of \cref{thm:multiplier-restriction-subadditivity}, and the graph argument for \cref{cor:multiplier-holomorphic-pullback}, are \cite[(15.1)--(15.3), pp.~158--159]{DemAnalyticOnline}. The restriction in \eqref{eq:multiplier-restriction} is explicitly the image ideal in $\mathcal O_Z$.

Strong openness is due to Guan--Zhou \cite{GZ15Strong}. The complete published proof in Sections 3.1--3.2, pp.~609--611, and the monotone extension in Section 3.3, pp.~611--612, provide the curve-and-extension mechanism of \cref{thm:monotone-multiplier-stability,cor:strong-openness}. \Cref{lem:bounded-domination-curve} reconstructs the required curve by blowing up an ideal, and \cref{lem:curve-extension-norm-lower-bound} gives its coefficient estimate. The induction uses a fixed inner slice polydisc, on whose compact closure finitely many local integrability neighborhoods give a common index before extension. The constant in the moving-slice extension is independent of that index and its weight.

The zero-Lelong implication in \cref{cor:zero-lelong-trivial-multiplier-ideal} is a special case of Skoda's integrability theorem; compare \cite[Lemma 5.6(a), pp.~35--36]{DemAnalyticOnline}. The proof here derives it from the multiplier-order bound and point-value extension. For comparison with that source, its potential $\varphi=u/2$ has the same Lelong number when measured against $\log|z|$ as our $u$ measured against $\log|z|^2$, and its weight $\mathrm e^{-2\varphi}$ equals $\mathrm e^{-u}$.

For discrepancy, change of variables and the general valuative criterion compare \cite[Proposition 10.12, Theorem 10.13 and Corollary 10.18, pp.~44--46]{Bou23Notes}, the version dated 11 September 2023. Its $\mathrm e^{-2\varphi}$ and $\log|z|$ convention is converted as above. \Cref{thm:general-valuative-multiplier-criterion} specializes the proof to a holomorphic numerator and transfers integrability using one ideal $\mathcal I(m\varphi)$ and the elementary split of the integral. The strict finite-resolution threshold includes the strict transforms of base divisors; the general criterion keeps one positive parameter uniform over all divisors.

The logarithmic cutoff-sum calculation is \cite[Lemma 3.5, p.~15]{DemRegOnline}. Its overlap construction, Lemma 3.6, pp.~16--17, is explained by the more general Lemma 4.6 and its proof, pp.~19--22. The exact common-potential comparison and maximum patching in \cref{lem:geometry-uniform-kernel-overlap,lem:maximum-cutoff-patching} reconstruct the argument of Vu--Xia \cite[Lemmas \texttt{patching} and \texttt{regularization}]{VuXiaNakamaye}. The proof of \cref{thm:quantitative-lower-bound-regularization} keeps the two conclusions of that lemma and the dependence of its curvature constant only on the fixed geometry.
